title: Core Web Vitals Explained in Plain English: LCP, INP, CLS
excerpt: What LCP, INP and CLS measure, the official thresholds, where to find your real numbers, the fixes that work, and how much Core Web Vitals affect rankings.

content_html:
You paste your homepage into PageSpeed Insights and get back three acronyms, a score out of 100, and a list of suggestions that reads like a developer's to-do list. Somewhere near the top, it says your page fails the Core Web Vitals assessment.

Is that an emergency or a footnote? Core Web Vitals are Google's three measures of how a page feels to a real visitor: how fast the main content appears, how quickly the page reacts when someone taps or clicks, and whether things jump around while it loads. They matter, just not in the way most panicked forum threads suggest.

This guide explains each metric in plain English, gives you the official thresholds, shows where to find your real numbers, and covers the most common fix for each one. If you are working through a full technical SEO audit checklist, this is the performance step.

What Core Web Vitals actually measure

There are three metrics. Each one has a "good" threshold that Google publishes, and each covers a different part of the experience.

MetricWhat it measuresGoodIn plain English
LCP (Largest Contentful Paint)Loading2.5 seconds or lessHow long until the biggest image or text block in view appears
INP (Interaction to Next Paint)Responsiveness200 milliseconds or lessHow long the page takes to visibly react after a click, tap or key press
CLS (Cumulative Layout Shift)Visual stability0.1 or lessHow much the layout moves around unexpectedly

A page passes when it meets all three "good" thresholds at the 75th percentile of real visits. In other words, at least three out of four page loads need to be at or better than each target. Google's Web Vitals overview on web.dev sets out these thresholds and the 75th percentile rule, measured separately for mobile and desktop.

One update to be aware of: INP replaced First Input Delay (FID) as a Core Web Vital in March 2024. If an article or tool still talks about FID, it is out of date.

Field data vs lab data: why your numbers disagree

You will see two kinds of numbers, and they often disagree. That confuses a lot of site owners, so it is worth getting straight.

  • Field data comes from real Chrome users visiting your site, collected in the Chrome UX Report (CrUX) over a rolling 28-day window. It reflects real devices, real networks and real behavior.
  • Lab data comes from a single simulated page load, usually run by Lighthouse on a throttled mid-range phone profile. It is repeatable, which makes it good for debugging.

For Search, the numbers that count are the field data, not the Lighthouse score out of 100. The Performance score is a lab diagnostic. It is useful, but it is not what Google's Core Web Vitals report is built on.

Say you run a bakery site with 40 pages. PageSpeed Insights shows a lab LCP of 4.1 seconds, but the field LCP is 2.2 seconds because most of your customers browse on recent phones over good connections. You pass. The lab number still tells you where the slow parts are, so it is worth acting on, but it is not a failing grade.

Small sites often have no field data at all, because CrUX needs a minimum amount of traffic before it reports anything. In that case, use lab data as your guide and focus on the fixes below.

Where to check your Core Web Vitals

Google Search Console

The Core Web Vitals report in Search Console uses field data and groups similar URLs together, rated Poor, Need improvement or Good, separately for mobile and desktop. A group's status is set by its worst metric, so a group with good INP but poor CLS shows as Poor. Only indexed URLs appear.

This is the best place to start because it shows patterns. If 300 blog posts are all in one "Poor CLS" group, the cause is almost always the shared template, not 300 separate problems.

PageSpeed Insights

PageSpeed Insights shows field data for the specific URL (and the whole origin) at the top when enough data exists, then a Lighthouse lab run underneath. Use the top section to judge, and the bottom section to diagnose. The lab report also names your LCP element and lists the elements that shifted, which saves a lot of guessing.

Actions

  • Open the Search Console report and look at mobile first, since that is usually where problems are worst.
  • Note which metric is failing and which URL groups are affected.
  • Open one example URL from each group in PageSpeed Insights to find the cause.

LCP: get the main content on screen faster

The LCP element is usually the hero image, a large banner, or the main headline. LCP gets slow for four common reasons: the server responds slowly, the image is huge, the browser discovers the image late, or render-blocking CSS and JavaScript hold everything up.

A typical example: a homepage hero is a 2.4 MB photo straight off a camera, it is set as a CSS background (so the browser finds it late), and a plugin has added lazy loading to it. All three slow down LCP.

The fastest LCP wins usually come from the hero image itself. Here is what to do:

  • Resize and compress the hero image, and serve a modern format such as WebP or AVIF. Our guide to image file size and formats covers this in detail.
  • Never lazy-load the LCP image. Lazy loading is for images below the fold.
  • Use a normal <img> element rather than a CSS background, and consider fetchpriority="high" on it so the browser requests it early.
  • Reduce server response time with page caching or a CDN, especially on shared hosting.
  • Cut or defer render-blocking scripts and stylesheets that are not needed for the first screen.

Google's guide to optimizing Largest Contentful Paint breaks LCP into stages so you can see which one is eating the time.

INP: make the page respond quickly

INP looks at the clicks, taps and key presses during a visit and reports roughly the slowest one. If someone taps your menu button and nothing visibly happens for half a second, that is a bad INP.

The usual cause is JavaScript keeping the browser's main thread busy. Chat widgets, tag managers loaded with many tags, ad scripts, sliders and heavy page builders all compete for the same thread. While the browser is busy running them, it cannot respond to the visitor.

Say a local plumber's site loads a chat widget, two analytics tools, a heatmap script and a booking plugin on every page. The "Call now" button feels sluggish on mid-range phones, even though the page looked loaded.

Most INP problems on small business sites are fixed by running less JavaScript, not by tuning it.

  • List every third-party script on the site and remove the ones nobody uses any more.
  • Load non-essential scripts (chat, heatmaps) later or only on the pages that need them.
  • Show immediate visual feedback when a button is pressed, even if the work behind it takes longer.
  • Ask your developer to break up long JavaScript tasks and simplify very large pages with thousands of elements.

Heavy JavaScript can also stop Google from seeing your content properly, which is a separate problem covered in our guide to how JavaScript rendering affects SEO.

CLS: stop the page from jumping

CLS measures unexpected movement. You go to tap "Book now", a banner loads above it, the button moves, and you tap "Call us" instead. Shifts that happen right after a user's own input do not count; this metric is about movement nobody asked for.

Common causes:

  • Images, videos and iframes without width and height attributes, so the browser does not know how much space to reserve.
  • Ads, embeds or review widgets injected into the page without a reserved slot.
  • Cookie or promo bars that push content down instead of overlaying it.
  • Web fonts that swap in late with very different sizing.

Reserve space for everything before it loads. Add width and height to every image and embed (CSS can still make them responsive), give ad and widget containers a minimum height, and show banners as overlays at the top or bottom of the screen.

Mobile is where Core Web Vitals usually fail

Phones have slower processors and often slower connections, so mobile scores are usually worse than desktop. Search Console reports mobile and desktop separately, so check both, but start with mobile, where problems tend to show up first. Our mobile-first indexing checklist covers the rest of what needs to work on phones.

Test on a real mid-range phone once in a while, not just on your laptop. A page that feels instant on office Wi-Fi can feel very different on a three-year-old phone on mobile data.

How much do Core Web Vitals matter for rankings?

Google says Core Web Vitals are used by its ranking systems, but there is no single "page experience signal". Its page experience documentation also says good scores do not guarantee top rankings, and that Google will still show the most relevant content even when its page experience is weak. Where many pages are similarly helpful, a better experience can contribute to success.

Treat Core Web Vitals as something that stops you losing, not something that makes you win. A fast page with thin content will not outrank a genuinely useful one. But if you and a competitor are equally relevant, a page that loads slowly and jumps around is giving away an advantage, and it frustrates the visitors you worked to attract.

Page experience is also wider than speed. A site that works for everyone, including people using screen readers or keyboards, tends to be a better experience overall. See where accessibility and SEO overlap for that side of it.

A simple Core Web Vitals workflow

  1. Open the Core Web Vitals report in Search Console and start with mobile.
  2. Pick the Poor URL group that covers your most important pages (product, service or lead pages before old blog posts).
  3. Run one example URL through PageSpeed Insights and identify the failing metric and its cause.
  4. Fix the cause in the template or theme, so every page in the group benefits.
  5. Click "Validate fix" in Search Console. Because field data covers a rolling 28 days, expect confirmation to take about four weeks.
  6. Look for site-wide patterns with a crawl. A free desktop crawler like Scary Spider SEO flags images over 100 KB, images missing width and height, and pages with slow server responses across the whole site, which are common contributors to LCP and CLS problems.

The bottom line

Core Web Vitals come down to three questions: does the main content show up quickly, does the page respond when someone uses it, and does it stay still while loading? The targets are LCP of 2.5 seconds or less, INP of 200 milliseconds or less, and CLS of 0.1 or less, measured on real visits at the 75th percentile.

They are a real ranking input, but a modest one next to relevance and content quality. Fix the template-level problems behind your Poor URL groups, starting with mobile and your most valuable pages, and do not chase a perfect lab score for its own sake.

Your next step: open the Core Web Vitals report in Search Console today, note which metric fails on mobile, and run one affected URL through PageSpeed Insights to find its LCP element or shifting elements.

faqs.question: Are Core Web Vitals a Google ranking factor?
faqs.answer: Google says Core Web Vitals are used by its ranking systems as part of page experience. They do not override relevance, so a slower page with clearly better content can still rank above a faster one. They matter most when competing pages are similarly helpful.

faqs.question: Why does Search Console say no data is available for Core Web Vitals?
faqs.answer: The report relies on field data from the Chrome UX Report, which needs a minimum amount of real Chrome traffic per URL group. New or low-traffic sites often have none. In that case, use PageSpeed Insights lab results to find and fix problems.

faqs.question: Do I need a PageSpeed Insights score of 100?
faqs.answer: No. The score out of 100 is a lab measurement from a single simulated load and is not what the Core Web Vitals assessment uses. Aim to pass the three field thresholds instead of chasing a perfect lab score.

faqs.question: What replaced First Input Delay?
faqs.answer: Interaction to Next Paint (INP) replaced First Input Delay as a Core Web Vital in March 2024. INP looks at responsiveness across the whole visit rather than only the first interaction, so it gives a more complete picture.

faqs.question: How long does it take for Core Web Vitals fixes to show up?
faqs.answer: Lab tools show improvements immediately after you deploy a fix. Field data in Search Console is based on a rolling 28-day window, so expect around four weeks before the report fully reflects the change.
